newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss farmers seek compensation for mad cow loss.
newsitem.headline: Swiss farmers seek compensation for mad cow loss.

text.p: More than 2,000 Swiss farmers launched legal action against the federal government on Wednesday seeking compensation from Berne for financial losses stemming from the "mad cow disease" crisis.

Two farmers' groups from western Switzerland filed a formal complaint that aims to force Berne to take responsibility for losses that have piled up since the disease began crimping Swiss beef sales, a spokesman for the Swiss Farmers' Association said.

The UPS and Agoro groups demanded 36 million Swiss francs ($24.9 million) in compensation for losses the 2,165 farmers incurred in 1996. Swiss farmers lost a total of around 350 million Swiss francs ($242 million) overall last year, and a similar loss is expected this year.
"With this action, UPS and AGORA demand that the federal government recognise its legal as well as financial responsibility in this matter," AGORA said in a statement.
"Not least we would like to force the government to draw the necessary conclusions so that further crises in the sensitive area of nutrition safety can be avoided in the future."

Around 240 cases of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) -- a brain-wasting illness that may be fatal to humans who eat infected meat -- have been reported in Switzerland, putting it second only to Britain.

The farmers blame the government for waiting too long to adopt measures against the disease. Berne banned the use of animal meal as cattle fodder in December 1990. Britain did so in July 1988, and other countries followed suit a year later.
At the end of 1996, 23 countries were boycotting Swiss cows or beef, costing Swiss producers 140 million Swiss francs ($97 million) a year, the farmers' groups said. ($1=1.4465 Swiss Franc)
